sop.text:
I study how people who cannot see a screen can still tell when an AI is wrong—and what interface design can do when they cannot.

In a 14-participant diary study with blind screen-reader users, I asked how they verify LLM-generated answers [lib:cv]. The most common strategy was asking a sighted friend: exactly the dependence these tools were supposed to eliminate [lib:sop_draft]. That finding led me to build SourceSpeak, a browser plug-in that reads provenance cues aloud as a screen reader traverses an LLM response. In a within-subjects study (n=12), participants caught 2.3× more incorrect answers with the plug-in than without it [lib:cv]. The first-author paper from this work is currently under review [lib:cv].

During my internship at Microsoft Research Asia, I examined a related breakdown in a different population [lib:cv]. In a four-week study with 20 older adults (ages 65–82) and their adult children, I found that when a family member initiated the repair after a conversational agent error, the older adult's continued use of the agent doubled [lib:cv]. The takeaway I carry into a PhD: trust in AI systems is repaired socially, not just technically [lib:sop_draft].

These two projects share a structure—a population excluded from mainstream AI design, a failure mode invisible to standard evaluations, and a mixed-methods approach combining interviews and diary studies with an instrumented prototype [lib:interests]. That is the research program I want to pursue at Cornell.

Prof. Shiri Azenkot's empirical study of how blind and low-vision people use AI-powered scene description applications [paper:W4396833521] is the closest existing work to my SourceSpeak research; I want to extend her methods to provenance transparency and trust calibration across LLM interfaces. Prof. Kaitlyn Zhou's finding that LLMs' reluctance to express uncertainty harms user decision-making [paper:W4402671787] and her interaction-centered reliance framework [paper:W4411119305] would let me situate SourceSpeak's effects within a broader theory of human-LM reliance—exactly the theoretical grounding my prototype work needs. Prof. Aditya Vashistha's demonstration that AI writing suggestions homogenize toward Western styles [paper:W4409746764] points toward the cross-cultural questions my older-adult data raised; his active lab working with marginalized communities [advisor:Aditya Vashistha] would be the right environment to extend the family-mediation findings to other non-Western household contexts. Prof. Susan Fussell's work on a fact-checking chatbot in private messaging groups [paper:W4406258040] and on parasocial engagement with AI voice messages [paper:W4410513031] opens a complementary angle: how the social structure around a conversational agent shapes whether errors get caught and repaired at all.

Cornell Information Science's breadth across HCI, AI ethics, and CSCW, and the density of faculty working on trust and marginalized users, make it the environment where these threads can come together.

In a PhD I intend to design and evaluate interfaces that make AI provenance and errors legible to users who are routinely left out of design processes—blind and low-vision users, older adults in non-Western households, and others whose verification strategies current systems ignore [lib:interests]. I will use mixed methods and working prototypes, the combination that has driven both of my research projects so far [lib:cv]. My longer-term goal is a research position where I can continue this work and train others to do it.

Mei Lin
